Sportsbook Power Ratings vs. Media Power Rankings: Why They Don't Match

Published November 10, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Every Tuesday, a dozen outlets publish NFL power rankings — ordered lists running 1 through 32 built from the previous week's results, the eye test, and whatever storyline is dominating the news cycle. Bettors glance at those lists and sometimes get confused when the market doesn't seem to agree: a team jumps from 11th to 4th after one blowout win, yet the spread against its next opponent barely moves. That's not the market being slow. A media power ranking and a sportsbook's internal power rating are built from different materials, measured on different scales, and used for entirely different jobs — and mixing the two up is a quiet way to misread a line.

What a sportsbook power rating actually is

A sportsbook's power rating is a number, not a rank — typically something in the range of roughly 80 to 100-plus points per team, built from a blend of scoring margin, strength of schedule, situational factors like injuries and rest, and in most modern shops, a layer of predictive modeling on top of the raw box score. The rating exists for one purpose: subtract one team's number from the other's, add a home-field adjustment of somewhere around 1 to 2.5 points depending on the matchup, and the result is a proposed spread. It's an input to a calculation, not a publication meant to be read on its own.

Because it's built this way, the gap between two teams' ratings matters far more than where either team sits in some larger order. A team rated 96.5 is a true 1.5-point favorite over a team rated 95, regardless of whether those two teams are ranked 4th and 11th or 15th and 22nd on anyone's list. The rating is continuous and granular by design — it has to be, since it's feeding a number the book will stand behind with real money on both sides.

What a media power ranking actually is

A media power ranking, by contrast, is an ordinal list — a strict 1-to-32 ordering with no information about how far apart any two teams actually sit. The methodology varies by outlet, but it's generally some mix of recent results (often overweighted toward the last game or two), a subjective read of how a team "looks," and narrative momentum: a team that wins ugly can slide despite the result, while a team that loses a competitive game against a good opponent can hold steady or even climb. None of that is wrong for what it's trying to do — give readers a digestible, discussable weekly order — but it isn't trying to produce a number you can subtract from another number to get a betting line.

The core distinction: a power rating answers "how many points better is Team A than Team B, specifically." A power ranking answers "which of these 32 teams would a reasonable observer currently rather have," with no claim about the size of the gap between any two entries on the list.

Side by side: two systems, two jobs

Laid out next to each other, the two systems barely overlap in what they're built to do, who builds them, or how often they move.

DimensionSportsbook power ratingMedia power ranking
Output typeContinuous number per teamOrdinal position, 1 through 32
Built byIn-house quants and traders, often with proprietary modelsA writer or editorial panel
Primary inputScoring margin, schedule strength, injury/rest data, model outputRecent results, the eye test, narrative
Update cadenceContinuously, as new information arrivesWeekly, usually tied to a publishing schedule
Public visibilityNever published directlyPublished as the entire product
What a change actually meansA real shift in expected scoring marginCan be driven entirely by presentation, not substance

That last row is the one that trips bettors up most often. A media ranking can swing five or six spots off a single eye-catching result — a come-from-behind win, a lopsided loss to a bad team — in a way a disciplined rating model usually won't, because the model is weighing that one result against everything that came before it rather than letting it dominate the week's conversation.

A worked example with real numbers

Say a media outlet has Team A at No. 4 this week after a 31-point win, and Team B sitting at No. 14 after squeaking out a 3-point win over a middling opponent. Read as a ranking alone, that ten-spot gap looks like a real mismatch on paper. Now put hypothetical sportsbook ratings on both teams: Team A at 97.5, Team B at 95.5 — a gap of exactly 2 points. If they meet at Team A's stadium with a typical home-field adjustment of 2 points, the opening number comes out to roughly Team A -4. That's a competitive, single-digit line, not the lopsided mismatch a ten-spot ranking gap would suggest to someone reading the list at face value.

The blowout that vaulted Team A up the media list might have come against a bad opponent, which a well-built rating model discounts through its strength-of-schedule component; the ranking, with no such adjustment built in, has no way to express that nuance in its final-week position. Both systems can be internally "right" by their own logic and still tell two very different stories about the same pair of teams.

The mistake: treating ranking movement as rating movement

The specific error worth watching for is assuming that a big jump in the media power rankings should translate to a correspondingly big jump in the number, or vice versa. "They jumped from 12th to 5th, so the spread should move a lot more than it did" treats an ordinal list like it carries magnitude information it was never built to carry. A team can leap seven spots on a ranking list while its actual rating moves by half a point, because the move was driven by how the result looked rather than by anything that changes a predictive model's estimate of the team's true level.

If a line isn't moving the way a flashy week-over-week ranking jump implies it should, the ranking is very likely the thing out of step with reality — not the number.

Why books don't publish their numbers

Sportsbooks keep their raw power ratings internal for a straightforward competitive reason: the rating is proprietary modeling work, refined over years and reflecting a house's specific edge in weighing injuries, schedule, and situational spots. Publishing it would hand that edge to every other book and every sharp bettor shopping for a mispriced numbers. What the public does see is the output — the posted spread and total — which is the rating already converted into a betting line, home-field adjustment and market feedback included. Our guide to line shopping gets into how that posted number can still vary slightly book to book even when the underlying ratings are directionally similar.

What to actually do with both lists

Media power rankings are still useful — for context, for storylines, for a quick gut check on who's trending in the right direction — just not as a stand-in for the market's actual number. The more reliable read on any single matchup is the posted spread itself, since that figure already reflects whatever power-rating-style model the book is running, filtered through the adjustments and public betting action that shape a final line. Treat a big weekly ranking jump as a prompt to go check the actual number, not as information you can plug into a spread calculation on its own.

Frequently asked questions

Do sportsbooks actually call it a "power rating" internally?

Terminology varies by shop, but the underlying idea — a single number per team used to generate a spread through subtraction and a home-field adjustment — is standard across the industry, even if the exact name and formula are treated as proprietary.

Can I build my own power rating as a bettor?

Yes, and plenty of serious bettors do, usually starting from publicly available scoring-margin and schedule-strength data. The goal isn't to match a sportsbook's exact number but to spot cases where your own estimate and the posted line disagree enough to be worth a second look.

Why do different media outlets rank the same team so differently?

Because the methodology is largely subjective and outlet-specific — one writer might weigh the most recent game heavily while another looks at a four-week trend, and neither approach is wrong so much as differently opinionated. That subjectivity is exactly what separates a ranking from a rating.

Does the gap between power ratings and power rankings apply to other sports too?

The same underlying split exists anywhere a league has both a betting market and media rankings — NBA and NHL power rankings carry the same narrative-driven quirks relative to the number books actually post for a given game.

Is a reverse line movement the same thing as a ranking disagreeing with the market?

No — those are different phenomena. Reverse line movement is about the number moving opposite to where the majority of public bets are landing, which is a market-structure signal. A ranking disagreeing with the number is just two different measurement systems producing different outputs, with no betting signal of its own.
